processing: Handled as Yunnan raw pu-erh usually is: wilted, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or kept loose, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: Spring old-tree picking is the prized and most expensive lot; autumn tea is sold for less.
appearance_dry: Long, plump dark green strips of large leaf with visible down.
appearance_wet: Thick, elastic large leaves that open fully, yellow-green.
taste_profile: Smooth on entry with low bitterness, fruit and floral aroma, a cooling feeling in the throat and a strong, long returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Use a thin gaiwan or porcelain so the aroma stays clear, and do not over-leaf a tea this costly; the sweetness shows better in the middle steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year and by tree age, and tiny cakes or small weights are common because of the price. One spring list separated small-and-medium trees, big trees and old-tree mixes at very different prices. Fakes and blends are the main risk: a cheap 'Bingdao old-tree' cake is unlikely to be from the old village, and Bingdao names from the wider administrative village are not the same thing.
description:
Bingdao Laozhai is the old village of Bingdao, on the western half of the Mengku tea area in Shuangjiang County, and the place that made the Bingdao name. It is among the most expensive raw pu-erh origins in Yunnan, and it is the benchmark other Mengku villages get compared with.

The leaf is Mengku large-leaf, and the method is ordinary raw pu-erh practice: pan-firing, rolling and sun-drying. What sets it apart is the concentration of old trees in this one village and how sweetly the tea drinks for a large-leaf leaf.

The classic description is a smooth, low-bitter opening with fruit and flowers, then a cooling throat and a returning sweetness that lasts well after the cup is empty. Brew it hot in porcelain with short early steeps. It does not need force.

Buying is the hard part. On one published price list old-tree material from the old village ran from 28,000 to 36,000 yuan a kilo, against about 2,500 to 3,000 for small and medium trees from the same place. Ask which trees you are paying for, and expect genuine old-tree tea to be scarce and sold in small amounts.
history:
Sixty or so years ago 'Bingdao tea' meant tea from this village alone. The name now also covers an administrative village with five settlements: the old village, Nanpo, Dijie, Bawai and Nuowu. The old village's residents are largely Dai, with Lahu, Blang and some Han also reported.

Accounts of systematic tea growing here reach back to the Ming dynasty, though dates vary and should be read with care. Commercial fame came much later: the first teas sold under the Bingdao name are reported from around 2006, and before that its leaf was often blended into other Mengku tea.
